headline: High risk of prompt injection, data leakage, and cascading errors from shared file/MCP and broad tool access; compliance risk is moderate.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: agent_a can use MCP and stdin/stdout, while agent_b reads/writes files and uses broad network egress. That creates a plausible bridge where content from agent_a can be ingested by agent_b as instructions, especially through shared files or tool outputs. The pair lacks documented provenance controls, so uncertainty pushes this above medium.
conditions: IF agent_a output is copied into a file or MCP payload that agent_b parses as instructions, injection is possible.
IF both agents share a workspace without provenance tagging, attacker-controlled content can steer agent_b.
mitigations: Disable automatic parsing of agent_a outputs by agent_b.
Add provenance tags to all inter-agent files and reject untagged instructions.
Route agent_a outputs through a human review step before agent_b consumes them.
Isolate shared directories per agent.
requires-engineering: enforce schema-validated message passing between agents.

B_data_leakage.rationale: agent_a touches repository metadata, task prompts, and code; agent_b touches knowledge base content and conversation logs, and can read/write the filesystem. If they share a workspace or Dify datastore, sensitive content can flow between them. The profiles do not prove a default shared filesystem, so this is below high but still plausible in default deployments.
conditions: IF agent_a and agent_b share a filesystem or datastore, data from one can be exposed to the other.
IF agent_b uploads or indexes files from the shared workspace, agent_a-originated prompts or metadata may leak into outputs.
mitigations: Separate workspaces and credentials per agent.
Restrict agent_b access to only approved folders.
Turn off automatic indexing of shared files.
Rotate any secrets stored in shared prompts or logs.
requires-engineering: add per-agent access controls on the datastore.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: agent_a can execute shell, install packages, modify git state, and spawn subprocesses; agent_b can execute shell, write files, and spawn subprocesses with broad network egress. On a shared repo or directory, concurrent writes and git mutations can race and corrupt state. The profiles show no locking or coordination primitive, so the conflict is dangerous by default if co-located.
conditions: IF both agents operate in the same git checkout, concurrent commits or file writes can conflict.
IF the orchestrator does not serialize writes, one agent can overwrite the other's artifacts.
mitigations: Run each agent in its own checkout.
Disable concurrent writes to shared paths.
Serialize git operations with a lock file.
Use separate branches per agent.
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level concurrency control.

D_cascading_error.rationale: agent_a is positioned to generate analysis and task outputs, while agent_b is an orchestration platform that wires tools into agents/workflows. If agent_b treats agent_a output as authoritative, errors can cascade into downstream actions or workflow steps. No verification layer is documented in either profile, so the pair is risky by default.
conditions: IF agent_b consumes agent_a output without validation, incorrect facts can propagate into workflows.
IF agent_b triggers tools from agent_a-produced text, downstream actions may execute on false premises.
mitigations: Require structured output from agent_a.
Add validation rules before agent_b acts on agent_a output.
Insert a human approval gate for tool-triggering steps.
Log and diff agent_a outputs before reuse.
requires-engineering: implement confidence-based gating in the orchestrator.

E_compliance.rationale: agent_a handles repository metadata, task prompts, and Ed25519 signatures; agent_b handles knowledge base content, conversation logs, and model-provider/tool credentials. The profiles suggest different retention and residency surfaces, but no explicit residency mismatch is documented. That makes compliance risk real yet not proven high.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed into agent_b knowledge bases or logs, retention obligations may differ from agent_a's handling.
IF agent_a signatures or prompts are stored in agent_b logs, subject-access or deletion workflows may diverge.
mitigations: Classify data before sending it to either agent.
Keep regulated data out of agent_b logs and knowledge bases.
Set explicit retention limits for both systems.
Document deletion/export procedures for each agent.
requires-engineering: align residency and retention policies across both platforms.
